new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (PNG page scan, 1390x2072, printed p. 283 = PDF page 5 of the 16-page assembled PDF, which has no text layer) and read the page image directly: under section '1.2. Remarks' (heading on p. 282), remark '7) The first syllable of a radical or a stem seems to be stressed.' is there exactly as quoted, between remark 6 (low-toned u deletion between consonants) and remark 8 (nasalised voiced consonants unattested). Persée's scanned text (line 75) has the same sentence. Persée landing page confirms Musamba Chanda V., 'Notes on Wongo Phonology and Morphology', Africana Linguistica 10 (1986), pp. 279-294, DOI 10.3406/aflin.1986.930, open on Persée, so status statement found in an open source i…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Wongo is a tone language (high tone marked; sec. 2.11 describes Non-Predicative vs Predicative tone shapes of words). Alongside tone, the author notes tentatively that stress falls on the first syllable of the radical/stem, i.e. on the first syllable after the (nominal or verbal) prefixes: a morphologically anchored root-initial stress. The claim is hedged ('seems to be') and given in a one-line remark without examples.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the author says the paper's conclusions are 'provisional' (p. 281).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (radical/stem); the transcription convention (p. 281, conv. 19) marks high tones, not stress, and no stress marks appear in the examples. Data from a single informant (Kumarer Nyeth) collected 1976-1978 at Lubumbashi.
new_statements.identity_note: Chanda 1986 describes the Isiinkere dialect (isíiŋkeRé, 'language of the lower area'), which the Wongo regard as the basic/'true' Wongo, from one informant (Kumarer Nyeth, village Ikwiti, Idiofa/Gungu zones); Glottolog has no separate dialect code, so it maps to wong1247 itself. The unopened theses cover the Kilembe (Paukindambi 1977) and Kipuku (Ilundu Kawey 1985) dialects.

sources.note: Section 1.2 'Remarks', remark 7, p. 283: 'The first syllable of a radical or a stem seems to be stressed.' Language is tonal (H tone marked, sec. 2.11 'Tonal behaviour of words', pp. 292-294); nothing on secondary stress. Persée's PDF download is altcha-gated, so the article was saved as the 16 per-page scans plus Persée's scanned text.
